speaker: Sholto Douglas
title: Is RL + LLMs enough for AGI? — Sholto Douglas & Trenton Bricken
question: In frontier LLM architecture design, why do simple hardware-constrained changes routinely outperform more elaborate algorithmic innovations?
guest: They very clearly understand this dance between the hardware systems you're designing the models around and the algorithmic side of it, so the models feel perfectly designed up to their constraints. If you diff the base transformer to DeepSeek V2 and V3, you can see them running up against the memory bandwidth bottleneck in attention. Initially they do MLA, trading FLOPs for memory bandwidth, and then NSA, where they more selectively load memory bandwidth. You see a similar thing with their approach to sparsity, iteratively working out the best way over multiple papers. The part I like is that it's simple. A big failure mode a lot of ML researchers have is doing overly complicated things that don't think hard enough about the hardware systems you have in mind. For their first MoE solution, they designed rack- and node-level load-balancing losses, and then came up with a much better solution later without an auxiliary loss, just using bias terms. Balancing an auxiliary loss is annoying because you force the model to trade off against the main objective and tune loss coefficients, whereas the bias is cleaner.

points.core: Effective architectures co-design algorithms directly around hardware bottlenecks like attention memory bandwidth.
points.note: Accept: tailoring model architecture to concrete accelerator constraints such as memory bandwidth, KV-cache loading, or rack/node interconnects. Do not credit: generic claims that faster hardware helps AI.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The core reason is that at frontier scale, the binding constraint is compute throughput, not algorithmic cleverness. This is essentially Sutton's "Bitter Lesson" combined with Sara Hooker's "hardware lottery": methods that best exploit available hardware win, because they let you train bigger models on more data for the same budget.

Simple changes that align with hardware (dense matrix multiplies, parallelizable attention, pre-normalization, lower precision, cache-friendly layouts) translate directly into more tokens processed per dollar. Elaborate innovations often introduce irregular memory access, sparsity, dynamic control flow, or sequential dependencies that run poorly on GPUs and their heavily optimized kernels, so their theoretical gains vanish in wall-clock terms.

Several further factors compound this. Many algorithmic wins shown at small scale shrink or disappear at large scale, where data and parameters let the model learn what the inductive bias was meant to supply. Complex mechanisms also interact unpredictably with optimization stability, distributed training, and inference serving, raising engineering risk. And the standard stack has years of accumulated tuning, so any newcomer competes against a deeply optimized baseline.

The premise is a strong tendency, not a law: the transformer itself was an algorithmic innovation, though one that succeeded partly because it parallelized well.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Frontier LLM training and inference are governed not by abstract FLOP counts, but by wall-clock throughput under fixed cluster budgets. Modern GPUs and TPUs pair immense matrix-multiplication capacity with comparatively scarce memory bandwidth, on-chip SRAM, and interconnect speed. Elaborate algorithmic innovations often introduce irregular memory access, sequential dependencies, or non-matmul operations that starve tensor cores and trigger costly off-chip memory transfers. Even when a complex design improves loss per FLOP at small scale, low hardware utilization makes it lose at equal time and cost, while intricate inductive biases frequently wash out as scale increases.

Conversely, simple hardware-aligned changes, such as FlashAttention keeping intermediates in fast SRAM, Grouped-Query or Multi-Head Latent Attention shrinking the KV cache, and coarse Mixture-of-Experts preserving dense matrix blocks, relieve physical bottlenecks while keeping tensor cores saturated and distributed parallelism clean. Under neural scaling laws, those throughput gains translate directly into training larger models on far more tokens within the same budget, routinely overpowering marginal per-step algorithmic cleverness.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The premise mostly holds, though it's an overgeneralization. The pattern has a few causes.

First, what matters is quality per unit of wall-clock compute, not per FLOP or parameter. GPUs and TPUs are fastest at large dense matrix multiplies and are often limited by memory bandwidth. A clever method that cuts FLOPs but causes irregular memory access, sparsity or awkward kernels can end up slower in practice. Second, many elaborate tweaks don't hold up at scale. Narang et al. (2021) re-tested dozens of Transformer modifications and found most gains disappeared under matched compute or different codebases. That fits Sutton's "Bitter Lesson": whatever scales cleanly with compute wins. Third, simple changes combine reliably, are less sensitive to hyperparameters, stay stable over long training runs and are cheap to engineer. At frontier budgets, those risks matter a great deal.

Sara Hooker's "Hardware Lottery" adds that ideas succeed partly because they fit current hardware. Still, the best recent advances are often clever ideas built around hardware limits rather than simple tweaks. FlashAttention, mixture-of-experts routing, and GQA/MLA KV-cache compression are examples. The real lesson is that ideas succeed when designed with hardware in mind.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Frontier LLM quality is governed primarily by scaling laws, meaning performance tracks effective compute and data processed far more closely than theoretical per-FLOP expressivity. Modern accelerators like GPUs and TPUs reach peak throughput only on dense, regular matrix multiplications with predictable memory access. Elaborate algorithmic innovations—such as intricate routing, custom recurrences, or exotic attention variants—often introduce irregular memory layouts, extra kernel launches, or synchronization barriers. Even when they cut theoretical FLOPs, they frequently stall on memory bandwidth or interconnect latency, slashing hardware utilization and raising wall-clock cost per token.

Simple, hardware-aligned changes like grouped-query attention or FlashAttention-friendly layouts instead maximize Model FLOPs Utilization, reduce memory movement, and compose cleanly with distributed parallelism. They also train more stably at scale and leverage mature compiler optimizations. Under fixed time and budget constraints, an architecture that converts more silicon cycles into stable updates trains on more tokens and achieves lower loss than a cleverer algorithm that leaves accelerators waiting on data.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
At frontier scale, a model’s cost depends on how efficiently it uses the hardware. Moving data through memory or synchronizing across GPUs can take longer than the arithmetic itself. An algorithm that saves FLOPs on paper can still slow the model down if it adds memory traffic, small GPU operations, or cross-device communication.

Simple changes often target the bottleneck directly. Grouped-query attention, for example, lets several query heads share key and value heads. That shrinks the KV cache and reduces the amount of data the GPU reads for each generated token, while preserving much of the quality of standard multi-head attention.

Those savings compound across layers and tokens. Within a fixed budget, they can buy more training tokens, longer contexts, or higher serving throughput. More elaborate innovations can win too. The test is whether they improve quality or throughput at the same end-to-end cost on the hardware that will actually run them.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
At frontier scale, the relevant comparison is model quality at a fixed training budget or serving latency. An algorithm can require fewer arithmetic operations and still run slower if it moves more data between memory and processors, leaves accelerators idle, or forces devices to wait for one another. A small architectural change that avoids one of those bottlenecks can pay off in every layer, at every training step or generated token.

Grouped-query attention illustrates the point. Sharing keys and values across several query heads shrinks the cache and reduces how much data the accelerator must read to generate each token. When memory bandwidth limits decoding, that simple change can improve throughput with little loss in quality. An elaborate innovation can win too, but its theoretical advantage has to survive implementation on real hardware and exceed the gains available from relieving the bottleneck directly.
